title: Complexity and measured costs
objectives: Count dominant operations and state the input/cost assumptions behind an asymptotic upper bound.
Design a repeatable local benchmark without confusing timing noise or setup choices with production guarantees.
Apply complexity and measured costs invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: An algorithm is a rule for transforming inputs into outputs. Its cost model says what operation we count and what input size means.

blocks.md: An algorithm is a rule for transforming inputs into outputs. Its cost model says what operation we count and what input size means. Let n be the number of list entries. If comparisons, indexing and fixed-size arithmetic are treated as unit-cost, one full scan makes n visits. A scan that exits on its first match can have a constant best case and a linear worst case. State which case and assumptions you mean; real Python large-integer arithmetic and expensive custom comparisons need a richer model.

For nonnegative costs f(n), saying $f(n)=O(g(n))$ means there are positive constants C and N such that $f(n)\le Cg(n)$ for all integer n at least N. It is an eventual upper bound, not an exact operation count or number of milliseconds. A tight order is written $\Theta(g(n))$ when an eventual lower bound of the same order also holds. The function 3n+7 is in O(n); it is also in the looser O(n²), so an O label alone does not assert tightness.

blocks.caption: Expected output: 8 8 28 3, then 16 16 120 4. The pair loop visits unordered distinct index pairs, n(n-1)/2, not n² exactly. The halving loop takes floor(log2(n)) steps for positive integer n in this code. Empty input needs separate boundary reasoning.

blocks.title: Compare counts before naming a winner
items: A scan over 8 items counts 8 visits; over 16 items counts 16. Doubling n doubles this count.
Pair counts grow 28 to 120 here, approaching a factor 4 as n gets large; the exact ratio is not 4 for every finite n.
Halving steps grow 3 to 4 for 8 to 16. Each size doubling adds one such step at these powers of 2.
Constants, allocation, data locality, comparison cost and workload can still make a small-n timing disagree with the large-n growth order.

blocks.md: Distinguish input storage, returned output and auxiliary workspace. An algorithm that returns n selected values needs output storage even if it scans with only a few extra counters. Copying a slice or sorting a new list can allocate memory. Do not call an entire operation constant-space after ignoring its copied inputs/output. A fixed number of arbitrary-precision integer counters is also not an absolute fixed number of bytes for unbounded values.

A benchmark must first verify the implementations compute the same contract. Choose representative sizes/distributions and name runtime, hardware and versions. Decide whether allocation, preprocessing, I/O and cache warmup belong in the measured boundary. Repeat measurements; a single noisy run is not a meaningful comparison. timeit measures a callable repeatedly and returns elapsed seconds. Its default treatment of garbage collection and setup must be understood for allocation-heavy workloads.

blocks.code:
from timeit import repeat
values = list(range(100))
samples = repeat(lambda: sum(values), number=1000, repeat=5)
print(len(samples))
print(all(seconds >= 0 for seconds in samples))
# Inspect samples to see this machine's total seconds per1000calls.
# min(samples) /1000 is the best observed per-call time in this setup,
# not a portable prediction or a measured production tail latency.
blocks.caption: Expected output: 5, then True. samples contains five actual elapsed totals for 1000 calls each; values are intentionally not hard-coded. Dividing a total by 1000 estimates average per-call time within that trial. The minimum is a best-observed local timing, not a guarantee, tail percentile or result on another machine.

blocks.md: For microbenchmarks, inspect repeats and explain noise rather than print many digits as fake precision. A production latency goal needs representative workload, concurrency, I/O and percentile measurements; the fastest repeat of sum(values) cannot prove it. When comparing algorithms, include the cost of sorting or building an index if the real use pays it. If preprocessing is reused over many queries, say how many queries amortize it rather than silently dropping that work.

Independent transfer: count comparisons for a scan that finds the first matching ID. Test first-position, last-position and absent targets for several n. Record best/worst case and cost assumptions. Then benchmark only implementations with the same returned answer, with and without one-time preprocessing inside the timed boundary. Report repeat data and environment, and do not claim an industry latency result from this local exercise.

Reference: [Python timeit](https://docs.python.org/3/library/timeit.html) for timing mechanics and caveats. The count formulas and asymptotic definitions above are derived or stated under the shown cost model, not claims about a production workload. Binary-search and list-insertion costs are taught in the next lesson.

blocks.caption: Experiment: compare constant, linear, n log n and quadratic growth across scales.

guidedExercise.prompt: What would be missing from a claim that one function is production-fast because its best tiny benchmark repeat was quick?
hints: Distinguishes a best repeat from production tail behavior.
guidedExercise.solution: The contract/correctness comparison, workload sizes/distributions, preprocessing/I/O, environment, concurrency and latency distribution are missing. Separate microbenchmark evidence from production requirements.

independentExercise.prompt: Write a small test case that deliberately breaks the contract boundary in "Complexity and measured costs" and verify how your implementation rejects or handles it.
hints: Test zero, negative, empty, duplicate, and boundary values.
Confirm both time/memory complexity and numerical precision remain within spec.

commonMistakes: The tight order refers to the stated counted operation and complete-scan contract, not an unspecified early-exit algorithm. (Both eventual linear lower and upper bounds hold.)
Big-O is a mathematical bound under a cost model. State tightness, case and measured behavior separately. (Tightness and real timings need additional evidence.)
An unfairly different contract or execution boundary can make timing numbers irrelevant to the real choice. (Correctness/contract checks come before timing claims.)
realWorldApplication: In practice, engineering teams apply complexity and measured costs within Algorithmic Invariants and Counterexamples when building reliable dsa and algorithms workflows — specifically to count dominant operations and state the input/cost assumptions behind an asymptotic upper bound.
quantFinanceApplication: Desk workflows in Algorithmic Invariants and Counterexamples rely on complexity and measured costs across dsa, algorithms, complexity, keeping numerical estimates, risk bounds, and low-latency paths predictable.
summary: Define input size, counted operation, case and memory boundary.
Growth bounds are not exact timings.
Verify equal contracts before benchmarking, include paid preprocessing and report repeat/environment evidence without universal latency claims.

quiz.prompt: Under unit-cost visits, a complete scan of n entries visits each entry once. What is its tight visit-count order?
options: Theta(n), because the exact visit count is n
Theta(1), because a loop has one source line
Theta(n²), because every scan has two nested loops
Exactly n milliseconds on every machine
quiz.explanation: The tight order refers to the stated counted operation and complete-scan contract, not an unspecified early-exit algorithm. (Both eventual linear lower and upper bounds hold.)

quiz.prompt: What does an O(n) claim alone establish?
options: The code takes exactly n CPU cycles
Its runtime is identical on all data distributions
It is faster than every O(n²) program for every n
An eventual upper growth bound under stated assumptions
quiz.explanation: Big-O is a mathematical bound under a cost model. State tightness, case and measured behavior separately. (Tightness and real timings need additional evidence.)

quiz.prompt: Which comparison is meaningful before interpreting two runtimes?
options: Compare any fast routine with any slow routine regardless of output
Verify both compute the same required output on the tested cases
Delete input validation from just one routine without disclosure
Hide preprocessing for one side even when every request pays it
quiz.explanation: An unfairly different contract or execution boundary can make timing numbers irrelevant to the real choice. (Correctness/contract checks come before timing claims.)

quiz.prompt: What does the minimum of five timeit repeats describe?
options: A universal runtime on every CPU
The best observed repeat under that local setup
The average per-call time across all 5000 executions
quiz.explanation: Report what the timing actually measures, including repeat/number setup and runtime/hardware context. (Noise, setup and workload limits still apply.)

quiz.prompt: The shown unordered-pair loop uses n(n-1)/2 iterations. How many pairs does n=8 produce?
quiz.explanation: Eight choices of first position and seven other positions count each unordered pair twice, so 8*7/2=28.
